items.title: I scraped 803 companies sub-processors to investigate what AI native companies a…
items.summaryText:
I scraped 803 companies sub-processors to investigate what AI native companies are using for their infrastructure.. 

Some interesting findings from the last time I did this in March:

> 44% of companies list two+ model providers (up from 33%). Small n, but Anthropic grew twice as fast as OpenAI. 

> 86 pairs where each company names the other as a subprocessor (@AnthropicAI + @Cloudflare, @vercel + @spacexai)

> 33% of companies list an inference provider (up from 22%). @modal continues to crush. 

> Chinese models are primarily coming through video (think Bytedance) rather than text (at least on the subprocessor lists)

> @typesafeai is the breakout hit, going from 0 to many companies in a short period. 

Caveat: subprocessor lists tend to be a lagging indicator, but a sure shot way of knowing if the company is using something. 

You can find all the updated data, design and insights at deploygraph dot com. Feedback welcome!

items.title:
There are basically two kinds of companies to build right now.

1. Diffusion of…
items.summaryText:
There are basically two kinds of companies to build right now.

1. Diffusion of AI
This is the "vertical SaaS" of today. There are a bunch of different models for it (FDE company, rollup, horizontal product) but ultimately it all boils down to the same thing: get AI diffused very close to where the work is being done.

Profound, Cognition, Harvey etc. A lot of great companies will get built here.

2. Frontier of AI
This is where the really interesting action is. Use AI to accelerate scientific progress, then build products from that progress.

It is a harder category to see. But we are seeing a lot more of it at @spc:

- Externa is adding hundreds of new chemical building blocks to proteins, so you can engineer a drug to match the disease instead of settling for what nature gave you.

- Epana Bio is using genomics and AI to design autoimmune therapies that go after the cellular origin of the disease.

- VenomicsAI is doing AI-accelerated drug discovery from venoms.

- Equivariant is doing multi-physics modeling for the semiconductor industry.

(There are always picks-and-shovels for AI as well. Lots of amazing companies in that category.)

Category 2 is not well understood or much talked about externally. It should be because I think that is where the vast majority of model driven returns will come from.

metadata.bio: General Partner @SPC, Co-Founder @Bevel_Health | Ex: Early Eng @facebook, CTO @Dropbox, Board @Flipkart | Optimist, Builder, Dad

items.summaryZh:
现在基本上有两种公司值得去建。

1. AI 的扩散
这就是今天的“垂直 SaaS”。它有一堆不同的模式（FDE 公司、收购整合、横向产品），但归根结底都归结为同一件事：让 AI 深度渗透到工作实际发生的地方。

Profound、Cognition、Harvey 等等。很多伟大的公司会在这里诞生。

2. AI 的前沿
真正有趣的动作在这里。用 AI 加速科学进步，然后基于这些进步构建产品。

这是一个更难看清的类别。但我们在 @spc 看到了更多这样的公司：

- Externa 正在为蛋白质添加数百种新的化学构建块，这样你就可以设计出与疾病匹配的药物，而不是将就于大自然给你的东西。

- Epana Bio 正在利用基因组学和 AI 设计自身免疫疗法，直击疾病的细胞起源。

- VenomicsAI 正在从毒液中开展 AI 加速的药物发现。

- Equivariant 正在为半导体行业做多物理场建模。

（AI 领域也总有“卖铲子”的机会。这个类别里有很多了不起的公司。）

第二类没有得到很好的理解，外界也很少谈论。但它应该被谈论，因为我认为绝大多数模型驱动的回报都将来自那里。

items.title: I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this woul…
items.summaryText:
I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000.

Then I look at what my team does with the same AI.

Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to teams, built a CRM, and started reaching out.

Look at that and you might ask: Why would I need a team at all?

The chart seems to agree. On OpenAI's GDPval benchmark, AI went from beating human experts 12.4% of the time in 2024 to around 83% in 2026. That's the aggregate view of the future of work: gather a lot of data and extrapolate a trend line.

But the aggregate misses something. To see it, you have to get intimate: zoom in on one real situation, with all its messiness, and extrapolate from there.

We gave everyone at Every access to the same customer survey and the same AI models.

• I found an opportunity to sell to teams.
• @poojary_yash saw that first-time subscribers were churning because we send too much email.
• @dabrundage noticed that many of our readers feel lonely: they're excited about AI, but people around them think they're crazy.
• @jackcheng turned the results into a Claymation game show.

Could you ask Claude to produce what each of them found? Maybe. But generating possibilities is cheap. Knowing which ones matter is hard.

@hammer_mt ran an experiment to predict what I'd say in Slack. When Claude got 400 attempts, it produced an answer like mine 93% of the time. But when it had to rank its own answers, mine landed in its top 10% only around 60% of the time.

Each person on a team is responsible for a different part of the world. That responsibility narrows where they look, and their perspective helps them decide what matters enough to act on. A team explores more possibilities than a single default prompt, and it can take responsibility for what it finds.

The obvious objection: models will get better at ranking. I think they will. But people aren't frozen while that happens. Comparing 2026 Yash with 2027 Claude misses that there will also be a 2027 Yash, with another year of experience, using 2027 Claude.

As models improve and spread, they raise the floor for everyone. The default answer becomes the baseline. The value is in using your perspective and responsibility to push past it.

That's why I think we need to change how we measure AI. Instead of only asking how well a model performs on problems everyone agrees are worth solving, ask: How good is it at doing my work, from my perspective?

The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it.

I presented this at Thesis: 2027. The full talk is on the Every podcast:

metadata.bio: ceo @every | the only subscription you need to stay at the edge of AI

items.summaryZh:
当我看着自己在每周的碎片时间里用 Fable 5.2 做的那些事，我会想：这要是放在过去，得五个人、花 20 万美元才能完成。

然后我再看我的团队用同样的 AI 做了什么。

上周，我在会议间隙分析了我们的客户调研，为我们团队做了一个游戏，发现了把 @Every 卖给团队的机会，搭建了一个 CRM，并开始联系客户。

看到这些，你可能会问：那我到底为什么还需要一个团队？

图表似乎也同意这一点。在 OpenAI 的 GDPval 基准测试中，AI 在 2024 年有 12.4% 的时候击败人类专家，到 2026 年这一比例升至约 83%。这就是未来工作的总体视角：收集大量数据，然后外推一条趋势线。

但总体视角会漏掉一些东西。要看见它，你必须深入具体：放大一个真实情境，连同它的所有混乱，再从那里外推。

我们让 Every 的每个人都接触同一份客户调研和同样的 AI 模型。

• 我发现了向团队销售的机会。
• @poojary_yash 发现首次订阅用户正在流失，因为我们发送了太多邮件。
• @dabrundage 注意到我们的许多读者感到孤独：他们对 AI 感到兴奋，但身边的人却觉得他们疯了。
• @jackcheng 把结果做成了一个黏土动画游戏节目。

你能让 Claude 生成他们每个人发现的东西吗？也许可以。但生成可能性很便宜。知道哪些可能性重要却很难。

@hammer_mt 做了一个实验，预测我会在 Slack 里说什么。当 Claude 有 400 次尝试时，它生成出和我类似答案的概率是 93%。但当它必须给自己的答案排序时，我的答案只有约 60% 的时候能进入它的前 10%。

团队中的每个人都对世界的不同部分负责。这种责任会收窄他们关注的范围，而他们的视角会帮助他们判断什么足够重要、值得行动。一个团队比单个默认提示词能探索更多可能性，也能为其发现承担责任。

显而易见的反驳是：模型会越来越擅长排序。我认为确实会。但在这一过程中，人并不是静止不动的。把 2026 年的 Yash 和 2027 年的 Claude 相比，忽略了还会有一个 2027 年的 Yash，带着又多一年的经验，使用 2027 年的 Claude。

随着模型改进和普及，它们会抬高所有人的下限。默认答案会成为基线。价值在于用你的视角和责任去突破它。

这就是为什么我认为我们需要改变衡量 AI 的方式。不要只问模型在大家都认为值得解决的问题上表现得多好，而要问：从我的视角看，它把我的工作做得多好？

总体视角能向我们展示能力曲线。具体视角则帮助我们看见，在乘着这条曲线前行时，我们可能建造什么，以及我们可能成为谁。

我在 Thesis: 2027 上讲了这些。完整演讲在 Every 播客上：

items.title: A New Vision for Human Work After Automation
items.summaryText:

I'm Natalia Quintero, and at Every, our team of writers and builders use AI every day, so we can tell you how the frontier is shifting, what actually works, and what you need to know.

So last week a…
items.bodyText:
Hey, welcome back to the Every Podcast, where we talk about the future of work.

I'm Natalia Quintero, and at Every, our team of writers and builders use AI every day, so we can tell you how the frontier is shifting, what actually works, and what you need to know.

So last week at Every, we hosted our first ever conference, V.C.S.S.,

It was a full day of talks in Brooklyn featuring speakers from Anthropic, OpenAI, Notion, Lovable, Ode, and many more.

If you missed it, we'll have all of the talks available at every.to forward slash TV.

We built the whole day around one question.

What does great human work look like after automation?

Dan Shipper, Every's co-founder and CEO, closed the conference with his answer, which you'll hear later in this episode.

He took our quarterly customer survey results and built a custom CRM, then a video game, and then personally reached out to a pretty vast number of our customers.

In pre-AI terms, he did the work of about five people, a data scientist, a game developer, a marketer, an engineer, and a salesperson.

But instead, he did all of that work with a single clot subscription over the course of a single week.

And if you ask Claude what it sees in the same survey, you'll probably get a generic answer that anyone could get.

And that's actually Dan's point.

Great work is the perspective you bring to the model.

So for the podcast this week, Dan's closing talk from our conference thesis.

Enjoy.

Thesis, did everyone have a good time?

Woo!

Well, we gathered here to answer one question, which is what is the future of great human work after automation?

I hope you got some good answers today.

Did you get some good answers?

Yes?

Yes?

All right.

I wanna add my take.

Hopefully I can help bring it together a little bit.

So I really, I love this question.

And obviously, because we built the conference around it, it's really the question that we try to answer every day at every,

And what's really interesting about this question is you're really trying to predict the future.

And there's two, I think, real methods for predicting the future.

One is what I'll call the aggregate, where you gather lots and lots of data, and then you extrapolate a trend line.

And the other is called the intimate, where you zoom in on one real case or real situation, and then you extrapolate from there.

And in our culture, we tend to emphasize the aggregate.

The aggregate is objective, it's quantitative, and the intimate kind of feels a little bit anecdotal.

And the aggregate's also extremely powerful.

The reason we have AI is the aggregate, is for example, scaling loss.

We found that if you put more data and compute on one end of the system, you get more capability out.

And all of us here are here because we're riding that curve that you can see in the aggregate.

We also use the aggregate to answer this question that we have come here for.

What does work look like after automation?

A good example is GDP Val from OpenAI.

It's a benchmark which measures how good models are at doing economically valuable tasks.

And the way it works is they have a bunch of experts pick tasks from their job, real tasks, and they turn it into a prompt.

They give the prompts to a model, and they give a prompt to a human that's not using AI, and then blind experts pick which one is better, the human version or the AI version.

And the prompts are very, very detailed.

They look something like this.

And in 2024, with GPT-4-0, experts, or AI, won against a human expert 12.4% of the time.

In 2025 it was 47.6 and in 2026 it was about 83%.

This is with GPT 5.4, I'm sure it's higher now.

I'm sure this benchmark is saturated.

You look at that, an AI is beating a human 83% of the time according to blind human experts at expert work.

And I can also see this in my work, in the way that I work.

If we look at my week, last week.

We ran our quarterly customer survey.

And in the cracks of my calendar, in the middle of all of the things that I had going on, I analyzed the survey data in a way that once would have required a data scientist or a growth person to do it.

Like I asked a ton of different questions and got a ton of different reports and outputs.

I made a video game for the team to play.

So we played in our all hands game to compete to see who knew our customers best.

It was a live, real time video game.

I realized that there's actually a really interesting opportunity to sell every to teams from all of this work.

And then, as one does, I vibe coded my own CRM and started using that to reach out to people.

You may have gotten an email from me last week.

If so, apologies.

It's kind of stunning.

It's amazing.

But if you look at it and compare it to human work.

This is in 2020 terms like a data scientist, a game developer, a product marketer, an engineer, a BDR, and like 200, maybe 200K.

And I got all of this for free as part of my cloud subscription.

And you think about that, you really think about that, you look at a table like this and you are like, we are so fucked.

We are so fucked.

And, yeah.

To me, it does this thing that I've been calling it.

It creates an agency rupture because we identify ourselves with the things that we do, with the work that we do.

And if you see a model doing work like you do, it strikes at our sense of self.

And I also think that while the aggregate is a very useful lens, especially when it comes to new technology, it also misses things.

It can be misleading.

And you can only see what's missing if you get up close.

So let's do that.

So, again, we've got these two different ways of predicting the future of the aggregate.

Okay.

Let's go into the Intimate.

Let's see how things look in the Intimate where you zoom in on one real case, you really understand all the messiness of it and all the different interconnecting variables and then try to extrapolate from there.

So if you look back at this table,

and you think about my week last week, doing all of this, which would have taken five people in 2020, and I'm doing all of that work with a team of agents in the cracks of my week while I'm doing a totally other separate set of tasks.

I think that this is actually how a lot of people in this room are working already, and probably if you're not, you will be in the near future.

And it feels almost normal to work this way.

Like it's not even that remarkable that I analyzed my survey or built the vibe coder to see a master sent some cold emails with my agents.

But this was actually really not normal, even a few years ago.

So think about in 2022, like before ChetGPT came out, we only had GPT-3.

And there were a lot of people looking at this chart, this aggregate chart and saying, this is not gonna continue, it's just a stochastic parrot.

And a lot of other people were like, this is the end of all jobs already.

We're not gonna have any work to do in two years, it's all over, go to the bunker in New Zealand, that's it.

And for me and for every, we take this intimate perspective.

We try to be up close.

And so in 2022, I was using GPT-3

And I realized that it felt like if I extrapolated out from using that tool, it would feel like using a team of people in a couple of years just by using an AI.

So I wrote that rather than replacing individuals, recent advances in AI will empower them to make an impact on scale matching some of the biggest businesses, research labs, and creative organizations of today.

I really think that's true now.

You could see it if you put your hands in GPT-3 and used it and extrapolated it.

I want to try to do that again today here with all of us.

If we take this and how we're working today, what does that mean for the future of great human work and are we really fucked?

And what's really interesting is, again, if I look at this table in a vacuum, you might assume, like, why would I need a team?

I have a team, I've got the agents right here.

But there must be something missing from this table because I do have a team where we are 30 people.

And by the way, the team here did such a fantastic job on this conference, can we just give them a hand?

This incredible, incredible group of humans and their clods, but mostly the humans.

And so I think we can answer this.

If we answer this question, it's going to tell us a lot about this larger question that we're trying to answer.

And I want to zoom in even more on this particular customer survey that I ran.

So when we ran this customer survey, this Q4 customer survey.

I gave it to the team.

So everybody had access to the data and to do their own analysis.

And what I got out of it was, there's actually a really cool opportunity to sell every for teams.

and I made my whole custom CRM and I started emailing people.

But what Yash got out of it, and Yash is our go-to-market engineer, what Yash got out of it, he cares, he's a monomaniac about growth, about growing paid subs.

And what he got out of it was a lot of first-time subscribers to every churn after the first month because we send too much email.

And what Douglas, who is our head of marketing and put together this conference, what he got out of it was, actually a lot of our readers feel lonely.

There's this interesting psychographic of people in this room where we all feel like we love AI, we're using it for all these things, but everyone else at our work and in our lives kind of looks at us like we're crazy.

A lot of people in this room and a lot of people on our list come to us because we are the only place where we are like, yeah, you can do great stuff with this.

That is what Douglas found.

And Jack, who is a senior editor, he made a Claymation family feud game show explaining the results.

It's time for Survey Showdown.

And here's your host, Dan Shipper.

Thank you.

Thank you.

Tonight, the vibe checks take on the context windows.

Okay, the vibe check...

So...

Extremely informative, but also very fun.

And I want to reiterate, they used AI to do all this.

We're using the same survey, we're using the same cloud, but different people on the team found very, very different and important things that they emphasize.

And that's kind of interesting because if you look at what Claude says, because anyone can hand Claude this survey, what Claude says about the survey with just a default prompt, which is just like what do you see in the data, it says the writing is the business, the bundle is what makes people stick, the risk is focused, the risk is focused and too much volume.

And all of this is actually, it's true.

These are real insights.

But everybody has access to this now, and so it's cheap.

And so not a single person on the team just submitted a response to this survey that looked like the default response.

They all did something very different.

And I think that's really, really interesting to pull on.

And another really interesting part of this is for each of these people on the team, they did all of this analysis while getting prepared for this event.

And everybody knows if you've ever put together a conference, it is like an all-consuming thing.

And still, Yash and Douglas, for example, who are intimately involved in every part of this, did their own analysis and came up with interesting things.

And Yash, for example...

He did the analysis and he wrote a PR to make the change to move the number that he wanted to move.

And while he was doing that, he was also helping build the live stream experience for this event, which is crazy.

If you have not seen this, we live streamed the entire thing with this custom video player that thousands and thousands of people were watching all day.

It's really amazing and he did that.

I think he had some help but he did a lot of that and he did it while doing this analysis that took him to do.

I know what you may be thinking is, well, couldn't I just have prompted Claude for what Yash and Douglas and Jack found?

And I think that's a really interesting question.

And the answer is yes.

We've actually experimented with this.

So Mike Taylor, who's our head of evals, tried to figure out if he could predict what I would say in Slack.

And the answer is yes, he can predict what I would say in Slack.

But there's an interesting caveat, which is he can only do it...

He can do it 93% of the time, but there's an interesting caveat, which is he can only do it if Claude can give 400 answers for each question.

So, Claude knows when it's trying to predict something in Slack, if Claude can give 400 answers at the same time, one of the things I'm going to say is in there.

But it can't rank them.

If you ask Claude to rank them, the thing that I say is only in the top 10%, like 60% of the time.

So, it's kind of a coin flip.

That's really interesting because it means we're getting into this world where, yeah, I could, you know, Claude can predict what I would do or I could get the output that Yash got or Jack got or Douglas got.

Generation is really cheap, but ranking is hard.

I actually wouldn't be able to find it in all of the noise that I'd have to sort through in order to get the thing that they would get.

Okay.

And that should tell you something really important about why teams are valuable in AI and ultimately why humans are valuable in AI.

If you're on a team,

and you're a human, and all of us are humans.

You have a responsibility for a particular area of the world that helps you narrow down what you look for, like how you prompt the model.

And then you have your own perspective.

You have a perspective that determines what you pick out of that world and call important, and call important enough to take responsibility for or take action on.

And,

I think if you want to look at it this way, for all of us who analyzed this survey last week, there were millions and millions of different paths available in the data, millions and millions of different insights we could have pulled out.

And our responsibilities, the things that we are responsible for in the business, helped to narrow down where we look or where they looked.

And our perspective lights up a few of those.

It helps us to rank those things.

And then you pick one and you take it forward.

And you've gone from this, you know, millions and millions of latent possibilities to one thing that you're the only one who would rank that because it's you.

It's the thing that lights up for you.

And if you zoom out, you know, we just went through one person doing that.

A team allows you to explore a much, much larger space of possibilities where each person has a perspective that allows them to rank and filter the parts of the world that they care about based on their responsibility and their perspective.

And that's much more powerful than whatever the default answer I would get from a default prompt.

And that's why it's really valuable to have Yash or Douglas or Jack or anybody else on the team accessing the survey data and pulling the insights out rather than just being like, what would Yash think of this?

And then I know what you're thinking.

Okay, Claude can't rank now, but give it a year.

It probably will be able to rank.

And I think that that is probably true.

it probably will get a lot better at ranking.

And if we ask that question, we probably would set it up something like this.

2027 Cloud's going to be a lot better at ranking.

How is 2026 Yash going to fare versus 2027 Cloud?

And...

I think if you really look at this, both sides of this equation are totally rigged.

So let's take it step by step.

First of all, why are we comparing 2026 Yash to 2027 Claude?

In 2027, Yash is going to be 2027 Yash with a whole bundle of new experiences and perspectives, and he's gonna be using 2027 Claude, I have no doubt.

It might be ChatGPT, it might be Gemini, but he's gonna be using a model.

Now we're like, okay, 2027 Yash versus 2027 Claude versus 2027 Claude.

And if you look at the 2027 Claude on the right side, someone had to set that Claude up.

I don't care if it's like a persistent agent or it's like you spun up some harness and it's off doing its thing.

Someone had to start it.

There's no immaculate conception of Claude happening in 2027, I don't think.

What you're really saying in this equation is we're comparing 2027 Yash with 2027 Claude versus probably the default prompt of 2027 Claude.

If you do that, now you start to realize, well, we've got 2027 Claude on both sides of this equation.

We can just cancel them out.

That's how math works in the intimate.

I don't make the rules.

But this is, like seriously, this is for real.

If you think about this, you actually are really comparing would I rather have 2027 Yash who's using this model or just the default prompt.

And Yash has a responsibility to a particular area of the world and a perspective, and the default prompt embodies the average answer, which we've already said everyone has access to, so it's not that valuable.

And my answer is I pick Yash every day.

I pick Yash every day, every time.

And I think that this, if you ask me why, the way that I would talk about this is we have to go back to when everyone has access to the model, whether it's 2026 Claude or 2027 Claude or 2028 Astra or whatever, it's going to be broadly distributed.

You've got Claude on both sides of the equation.

And because of that, that raises the floor for everyone and the default answers you get from the model, they look impressive to us right now, but because everyone will have them, they become not that valuable.

They're just, they're status quo, they're the baseline.

And yes, the floor keeps moving, but the floor keeps getting distributed to everybody.

And so what's valuable, the alpha, is where you push the model using your perspective and your responsibility for a particular area of the world.

And yes, that may get consumed into, that may get subsumed into tomorrow's floor.

as capabilities increase.

But if you're continuing to use the model, you're not frozen back in 2026 when you're using the old version of the model.

You're using that new model yourself.

And so those new capabilities rapidly become cheap, and what is actually expensive and rare is how you use them using your perspective.

And so now we've kind of started to get back to the question that we started with, which is if you remember the aggregate, from the aggregate alone, all you see is this line going up that looks like it's gonna replace all of us, and it looks like human work is going to zero.

And if you look at the aggregate from the intimate,

What we've started to find is that we have the same line, but humanity, human perspective, the way that we use the models rides on top.

And I think that is a more accurate view of how work will happen in the future with these models, than just saying, oh, we're just gonna get replaced because look at this chart.

And this is what I've been talking and writing about for several years now, this way of working and being in the economy called the allocation economy.

I wrote this article in 2024 where I wrote, you won't be judged on how much you know, but instead on how well you can allocate and manage the resources to get work done, the resources of intelligence.

You'll be allocating work to AI models and making sure the work gets done well.

And there are some really, really interesting implications if you believe this.

We're gonna be allocating work to models, and the default capability is distributed to everyone, so the responsibility and the perspective that you bring to the model is the thing that's valuable.

The first thing is, the first interesting flip is it should flip how we measure AI.

Right now when we measure AI capabilities, we measure them based on,

Consensus, is it good at problems that we all agree are worth solving?

So like math problems are easy because we can validate them.

Program problems are easy because we can validate them.

But again, by this logic, those capabilities are now distributed.

They are no longer as valuable.

And what we should be measuring instead is how good is it at doing my work from my perspective specifically?

And this is like kind of a weird flip.

It's a weird cultural inversion because I think for all of us, we have this feeling that getting to a settled answer or being able to use a settled answer or know a settled answer is where all the value is.

Like we're thinking about math and science and computer programming where your perspective doesn't actually matter.

And my view is that stuff has become much less valuable because it's commoditized.

And now the value comes from you having a non-consensus perspective that you can use to push the model to make something that you think is good.

And if you internalize that, then you start to think of things, think of model progress not as something that's going to replace you, but something that works for you, for your ends.

And as it gets better, so do you.

I think this is why the intimate matters.

When you look at what's going on in the aggregate versus the intimate, the aggregate has to freeze you.

It has to, in order to measure model progress, it has to freeze humans in 2020 and compare it to humans in 2020.

And I think the intimate empowers you to see what you might build and who you might become.

And we have all lived that perspective today.

This whole conference, this whole day, was about getting intimate with what it is like to work with these tools and work with other people, be with other people who are working with these tools.

And you all agree, you all know how valuable that is because if you could just look at a capability chart and know everything you needed to know, you wouldn't have come here.

I think now that the people in this room understand this and feel this, it's our job to go and spread it to the rest of the world.

Thank you.
